editorial.headline: A Nationally Open Café Activity That Bali Will Not Register for PMA
editorial.standfirst: Although nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, this café activity cannot be registered for PMA in Bali today.
editorial.body:
KBLI 56303 concerns a café or drinking-house activity built around drinks consumed where they are served. Its principal offer is hot or cold beverages for on-site consumption, rather than a particular menu, décor or service style. The premises may occupy either part or all of a permanent building. They may be fitted with equipment and facilities for preparing and storing drinks, or operate without those arrangements. What anchors the classification is specific: the principal provision of beverages, consumed at the business premises, within a permanent-building setting.

That definition speaks to the businesses registering the activity: operators whose main undertaking is providing those drinks for people to consume on the premises. The recorded scale availability is broad, spanning Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. Each is expressly open in the record, so scale does not narrow the national description of the activity. A business should nevertheless keep the classification’s centre of gravity in view. The code is framed around the provision of hot or cold drinks on the premises and the physical setting in which that provision takes place; those elements give the activity its identity.

At national level, foreign-investment treatment is clear. The PMA status is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership figure of 100%, cited to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Put plainly, the national record permits full foreign ownership for this activity. That matters because it makes the Bali position a separate geographic constraint, not a qualification of the national ownership ceiling. There is no lower national stake stated here: nationally, the listed ceiling remains 100%.

In Bali, the answer changes from ownership capacity to registrability. A foreigner cannot register this activity for PMA in Bali today. The Bali entry is a risk-class block: at the Besar scale, OSS places every scope at Low or Medium-Low risk, and the entry says this is blocked by the Bali moratorium of May thirteenth, two thousand twenty-six. The governing provincial rule is island-wide and permanent, blocking all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA. It should not be read as a Bali-side reduction in the 100% ceiling; the Bali record supplies no alternative percentage, but a categorical registration block. A nationally open, fully foreign-ownable activity is nevertheless unavailable for PMA registration in Bali under that moratorium.
